headline: Bunker Stack the Bay, Bonito Knock on Napatree's Door
subhead: Peanut bunker are thickening from Sakonnet to Watch Hill and the first bonito have crossed the state line — the albies won't be far behind.
body_markdown:
The bait tells the story on this shore before the fish ever do, and right now the story is bunker. Peanut schools that started the summer scattered and thin along the rocks have thickened into real bodies of bait working Sakonnet Point, Second Beach, and the mouth of the breachways at Charlestown and Weekapaug. Narragansett Bay has been pushing bunker out through the East and West Passages for two weeks now, and that spillover is exactly what's been loading up the water along Newport and Jamestown. Silversides are still in the wash on the calm mornings, and bay anchovies are showing thick enough in the breachway currents that the smallest fish in the food chain are finally worth paying attention to.

We flagged the bonito push last week, said the surge out of Block Island and Point Judith would keep spreading along the shoreline — and that's exactly what's happening. Bonito have crossed into Rhode Island water in real numbers now, working past Point Judith and showing up on the troll off the Sakonnet breakwater and outside Newport Harbor. They're still mostly an outside-the-breachway fish for now, but that westward creep toward Fishers Island Sound and the Race means Napatree and Watch Hill should start seeing them mixed with the bait balls any day. Albies haven't committed yet in this stretch — a few scattered reports of fish showing outside Sakonnet Point, nothing consistent enough to call a push into the breachways. September is when that flips, and with bait this dense, it won't take much.

Water's still sitting in that low-to-mid 70s range, warm enough to keep the striped bass staged rather than blitzing. That's the honest read right now — bass are on the bunker, but they're not organized. Boats working the mouth of the Sakonnet River and the rips off Newport are marking fish under the bait pods but getting more follows than committed strikes, which is a classic late-summer pattern before the water starts to slide. The moon builds to full on the 6th and 7th, and that's the trigger to watch. Tighter tidal flow around the full moon tends to bunch these loose bunker schools into something a striper can actually pin against structure, and that's usually when the first real blitz breaks open on this shore. If the pattern holds like it usually does, look for that within the next week to ten days rather than this weekend.

Bluefish have been the one bite you can set a watch by. Choppers are working peanut bunker and silversides hard off Second Beach, Sachuest Point, and the rocks below Fort Adams, and that's held steady through the warm stretch without any signs of slowing. Bucktails and metal — 1 to 2-ounce Deadly Dicks and Kastmasters — worked fast through the surface wash are getting hit as soon as they land when the blues are up. Chunked bunker fished on the bottom off the same rocky points is picking up bigger fish for anyone who wants to sit still instead of casting all morning. With bunker density building the way it is, expect the blue bite to carry through Labor Day week without much drop-off.

Fluke are doing what they do this time of year — thinning out of the back stretches. The upper Sakonnet River and the calmer stretches inside Jamestown have gone quiet compared to July, with the better fish sliding out toward deeper structure off Beavertail and the outside grounds near Newport. Anyone still chasing them should be working white Gulp on 3/4-ounce bucktails in 30 to 40 feet rather than the flats, and expect fewer fish for more effort from here into October.

On the rock structure itself, it's still a scup and bergall show more than a tog bite — green crabs dropped into the cracks around Beavertail, Brenton Point, and the outer ledges at Sakonnet Point are getting picked apart fast by scup and cunner, which is normal for early September before the blackfish really settle onto that structure. Worth scouting now, because once the water starts to slip into the 60s, those same ledges turn over to tog holding tight in the same cracks on the slack tide, and that bite builds through the fall.

Looking at the next few days, wind and tide matter more than anything else on this coast. If it stays light out of the south and southwest, work the breachways — Napatree and Watch Hill first — on the last two hours of the incoming, when bait gets pushed and concentrated against the rocks and any albies or bonito working the area have current to hunt in. Early morning remains the best window before boat traffic and sun push bait deeper. The bass game right now is patience: work bunker schools with a bucktail or a soft-plastic swim shad worked slow along the edge rather than through the middle, since fish holding under bait tend to peel off the sides rather than commit through open water. If the moon does its usual work and a cool night or two slides in behind it, expect the scattered stripers to organize fast, and the first real blitz of the fall to break open somewhere along this shore within the next week to ten days. Until then, this is a bait-first bite — find the peanut bunker, and everything else follows.
